# The External Affairs Power: s 51(xxix) of the Constitution

## 1. The issue

Section 51(xxix) of the *Commonwealth Constitution* lets the Commonwealth Parliament make laws "with respect to … external affairs". The question is how far this power lets the Commonwealth legislate on subjects that are not otherwise listed in s 51. Examples are land use, the environment, discrimination, criminal law and industrial relations, all of which traditionally fall to the States, including Victoria. The second question is what limits apply, as settled in *Commonwealth v Tasmania* (1983) 158 CLR 1 (the *Tasmanian Dam Case*) and later cases.

Once a valid Commonwealth law exists, it overrides inconsistent Victorian law to the extent of the inconsistency (*Constitution* s 109). It can do so by "covering the field", as in *Viskauskas v Niland* (1983) 153 CLR 280 at 292 (*Racial Discrimination Act 1975* (Cth)). So the reach of s 51(xxix) directly shapes how much legislative room the States have.

## 2. The scope of the power

The High Court has recognised four overlapping aspects of the power.

**(a) Matters geographically external to Australia.**
- Any law about a person, place, matter or thing physically outside Australia is within power.
- Authority: *New South Wales v Commonwealth* (*Seas and Submerged Lands Case*) (1975) 135 CLR 337 at 360 (Barwick CJ), 470–1 (Mason J).
- Confirmed in *Polyukhovich v Commonwealth* (1991) 172 CLR 501 at 528–31 (Mason CJ), 632 (Dawson J), applying to war crimes committed in Europe.
- Confirmed again in *XYZ v Commonwealth* (2006) 227 CLR 532 at [10] (Gleeson CJ) and [38]–[44] (Gummow, Hayne and Crennan JJ). There the Court upheld child sex tourism offences in the *Crimes Act 1914* (Cth) without needing a treaty.

**(b) Relations with other countries and international organisations.**
- *R v Sharkey* (1949) 79 CLR 121 at 136–7 (Latham CJ) upheld a sedition offence protecting relations with the King's other dominions.

**(c) Implementation of treaties.**
- *R v Burgess; Ex parte Henry* (1936) 55 CLR 608 at 640–4 (Latham CJ) and 681, 687–8 (Evatt and McTiernan JJ) recognised that the power extends to implementing international conventions, there the aerial navigation convention.
- *Horta v Commonwealth* (1994) 181 CLR 183 at 195–6 held that validity does not depend on the treaty being valid in international law.

**(d) Matters of "international concern".**
- This aspect was suggested in *Burgess* at 658 (Starke J) and 681, 687 (Evatt and McTiernan JJ), and in *Koowarta v Bjelke-Petersen* (1982) 153 CLR 168 at 216–17 (Stephen J).
- *Victoria v Commonwealth* (*Industrial Relations Act Case*) (1996) 187 CLR 416 at 485–6 left it open.
- It remains unsettled as an independent head of power.

**How treaty implementation reaches State fields.**
- In *Koowarta*, a 4:3 majority upheld ss 9 and 12 of the *Racial Discrimination Act 1975* (Cth) as implementing the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (CERD) (Stephen J at 216–17; Mason J at 224–9). This was so even though discrimination by private persons over Queensland land dealings was otherwise a State matter.
- The minority would have confined the power to matters inherently international (Gibbs CJ at 198–202).
- *Mabo v Queensland (No 1)* (1988) 166 CLR 186 then used s 10 of the same Act to invalidate Queensland legislation through s 109.

## 3. *Commonwealth v Tasmania* (1983)

**Facts.**
- The Western Tasmania Wilderness National Parks had been placed on the World Heritage List under the *Convention for the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage* (1972).
- The *World Heritage Properties Conservation Act 1983* (Cth) and regulations prohibited construction of the Gordon-below-Franklin dam.
- That dam had been authorised by the *Gordon River Hydro-Electric Power Development Act 1982* (Tas).

**Holding.**
- By 4:3 (Mason, Murphy, Brennan and Deane JJ; Gibbs CJ, Wilson and Dawson JJ dissenting), the key provisions were valid under s 51(xxix). This was so even though land management is quintessentially a State matter.

**Key propositions from the majority.**

1. **A bona fide treaty obligation is enough.** The subject matter of a treaty need not be "international" in some further sense. Entry into the treaty itself makes implementation an external affair (Mason J at 123–6; Murphy J at 171–2; Brennan J at 219–20; Deane J at 258–9).
2. **Broadly worded obligations can still bind.** Articles 4 and 5 of the Convention imposed genuine obligations despite being couched in terms of what each State Party would do "in so far as possible". The minority's view that they were merely hortatory was rejected (compare Gibbs CJ at 89–92).
3. **The "federal balance" is not a limit on power.** Following *Amalgamated Society of Engineers v Adelaide Steamship Co Ltd* (1920) 28 CLR 129, there is no reserved-State-powers doctrine. Mason J (at 127–9) held that the fact the power may enable the Commonwealth to legislate on matters previously left to the States is no reason to read it down. Gibbs CJ (at 99–100) dissented, warning that an unlimited treaty power would let the Commonwealth "destroy the federal balance".
4. **The law must conform to the treaty.** The law must be reasonably capable of being considered appropriate and adapted to implementing the treaty (Mason J at 130–1; Deane J at 259–60). Deane J framed this in terms of "reasonable proportionality". He would have read down or invalidated some of the more sweeping prohibitions that he considered went beyond protection of the listed property. Parliament nonetheless has a choice of means (Mason J at 130–1).

**Other limits illustrated by the case.**
- Deane J alone held that the scheme effected an acquisition of property requiring just terms under s 51(xxxi) (at 282–7).
- The majority disagreed: Mason J at 145–6 and Brennan J at 247–8. Their reasoning was that the Commonwealth acquired no proprietary interest.
- Even so, the case confirms that s 51(xxix) is subject to s 51(xxxi).

## 4. The main limits on the power

**(a) Bona fides: the treaty must not be a sham.**
- A treaty entered into merely as a device to attract legislative power would not support a law (Mason J at 124; Brennan J at 219–20; compare Stephen J in *Koowarta* at 217).
- This limit has never been successfully invoked, and the Court is reluctant to inquire into executive motives.

**(b) Conformity, specificity and "appropriate and adapted".** The *Industrial Relations Act Case* (1996) 187 CLR 416 is now the leading statement (Brennan CJ, Toohey, Gaudron, McHugh and Gummow JJ):
- **Specificity.** The treaty must prescribe a regime "with sufficient specificity to direct the general course to be taken by the signatory states". Merely aspirational statements will not do (at 486).
- **Test of conformity.** The law must be "reasonably capable of being considered appropriate and adapted" to implementing the treaty (at 487).
- **Partial implementation.** This is permissible unless the shortfall is so substantial that the law can no longer be characterised as implementing the treaty. Provisions that go beyond the treaty, or are inconsistent with it, are invalid (at 488–9).
- Applying these tests, some provisions survived (unfair dismissal implementing ILO Convention 158; minimum wages; equal pay). Others failed to the extent they were not supported by the treaty.
- *Richardson v Forestry Commission* (1988) 164 CLR 261 at 289–91 (Mason CJ and Brennan J) and 311–12 (Deane J) applied a proportionality analysis. It upheld interim protection of land pending World Heritage assessment because the protection was proportionate to the obligation.
- Listing decisions are effectively conclusive: *Queensland v Commonwealth* (1989) 167 CLR 232 at 239–42.

**(c) Express constitutional guarantees.**
- Section 51(xxix) is "subject to this Constitution". Laws made under it must satisfy s 51(xxxi) (just terms), s 116, s 117, s 92 and s 80 where relevant.

**(d) Implied limitations.**
- **Intergovernmental immunity.** A law may not discriminate against the States or impair their capacity to function as governments: *Melbourne Corporation v Commonwealth* (1947) 74 CLR 31; *Austin v Commonwealth* (2003) 215 CLR 185 at [124] (Gaudron, Gummow and Hayne JJ). In the *Industrial Relations Act Case* (at 498–504), provisions interfering with a State's choice of the number and identity of its senior employees, and with redundancy terms, were invalid on this basis. This was so despite treaty support.
- **Implied freedom of political communication.** It applies equally: *Lange v Australian Broadcasting Corporation* (1997) 189 CLR 520 at 567.

**(e) Characterisation and the "international concern" category.**
- Where no treaty exists, a law must still be characterised as being with respect to a geographically external matter, a foreign relation, or (possibly) a matter of international concern.
- In *XYZ* the dissentients (Callinan and Heydon JJ) urged a requirement of some connection with Australia, but this was rejected by the majority.

## 5. Competing arguments

**The narrow, federalist view.** This is the view of Gibbs CJ, Wilson and Dawson JJ in *Tasmanian Dam*, and of Gibbs CJ in *Koowarta*. It holds that the subject matter must be inherently international, because otherwise the executive's treaty-making power allows unlimited expansion of Commonwealth legislative power and erodes the enumerated scheme.

**The broad view.** This is the view of Mason, Murphy, Brennan and Deane JJ, endorsed unanimously in the *Industrial Relations Act Case* at 482–5. Its premises are:
- *Engineers* forbids reading down a power by reference to assumed State reserves;
- international relations have expanded since 1900; and
- the safeguards are found in conformity, specificity and other constitutional limits rather than in subject matter.

**Practical effect.** The broad view prevails. In practice, the "conformity" requirement does the work the federalist limits were meant to do.

## 6. Conclusion

Section 51(xxix) supports laws on geographically external matters, foreign relations and (probably) matters of international concern. Most significantly, it supports laws implementing bona fide treaty obligations, whatever their subject matter. *Commonwealth v Tasmania* settled that the Commonwealth may thereby legislate in fields otherwise within State competence, overriding State law through s 109, and that "federal balance" arguments do not confine the power.

The operative limits are:
- the treaty must be bona fide;
- it must impose sufficiently specific obligations, not mere aspirations;
- the law must be reasonably capable of being considered appropriate and adapted, or reasonably proportionate, to implementing the treaty (*Industrial Relations Act Case* at 486–9; Deane J in *Tasmanian Dam* at 259–60); and
- the law must comply with express guarantees (notably s 51(xxxi)) and implied limitations (*Melbourne Corporation*; the implied freedom of political communication).

These limits, rather than any subject-matter restriction, now define the boundary between Commonwealth and State legislative competence under the external affairs power.
